I was twelve in Kabul when soldiers took boys off the street.

I walked past the line of faces on my way home from school. Nobody stopped me.

That afternoon a rule got written inside me: if you are not always watching, always calculating, always three moves ahead, the people you love will be taken.

Here's the hard part. It worked. It got me out. It made me a provider for six people at twenty. It built a business from a folding table.

And thirty years later it was still running, long after the soldiers were gone.

What rule did your younger self write to stay safe? You don't have to answer here. Just notice if one came up.

posts.caption:
I was twelve years old in Kabul when soldiers started taking boys off the streets.

One afternoon I walked home from school past a line of boys' faces. Nobody stopped me. I kept walking. I didn't look back.

A rule got written inside me that day: if you are not always watching, always calculating, always three moves ahead, the people you love will be taken.

And I'll be honest. That rule worked. It got me out. When my father died, it made me the provider for six people at twenty. It built a business from a folding table at a flea market.

What I didn't know was that it would keep running for thirty years, in a safe house, in a safe country, with my wife and two sons who just wanted me to be in the room.

Most of us have a rule like that. It was written to protect us. The question is whether it's still needed.

What rule did your younger self write?

posts.theme: Story: the moment with my wife
posts.caption:
There's a moment I've never been able to forget.

My wife looked at me across a room, and I saw that she had stopped expecting anything from me. Not stopped loving me. Stopped waiting for me to come back into the room.

I was right there. I was providing, solving, planning three moves ahead, exactly the way a twelve-year-old in Kabul had taught me to. And I was completely gone.

That look did what no book had done. It made me ask a question I'd never asked: who is living this life?

In the same stretch I lost my business and nearly lost my family. The practice I found on a living-room couch at three in the morning is what gave my family back to me. Not overnight, and not perfectly. But really.

If someone in your life has stopped waiting for you to come back, I wrote the free book for you.

Every human being is wearing a costume.

The careful one. The funny one. The one who never needs anything. You put it on early, usually before you were ten, because it kept you safe.

The child doesn't call it a costume. The child calls it Tuesday.

So here's the question, and take your time with it: is it who you are, or is it what you had to become?

This is where my book Remembering Your True Self picks up. The person you became to survive is not who you are. It's where the diagnosis becomes a map, and the map becomes a move. It draws on neuroscience, psychology and contemplative traditions, and it tells you which claims are measured and which are belief.

If you haven't read the free one yet, start there. Both are on the site linked in my bio.

posts.theme: Course invitation 2: what waking up is not
posts.caption:
Waking up isn't bliss. Let me save you some money and some disappointment.

It's not permanent calm. It's not incense and robes. It's definitely not feeling a little taller than your brother-in-law at dinner.

What it is: the end of being completely fooled.

You still get angry. You still get scared. But an evening of it becomes twenty minutes. Then sometimes less. That's the honest version, and it's the only version I teach.

In the course, Awakening Your True Self, we practise exactly that, together, over twelve weeks. It's $297 one time. Some of what I offer is free and some isn't, and you need none of it to begin.

It's not a spiritual trap. It's a mechanical one.

Here's how it works. Wherever attention goes, a world seems to form around it. Put your attention on one critical email and within a minute you're living in a whole world where your job is in danger, your boss hates you, and you're about to be found out.

None of that happened. Attention built it.

That's actually good news. If it's mechanical, it can be seen. And something that can be seen can't fool you completely anymore.

Next time you notice a whole world forming around one small thing, try saying: "That's the movie, caught in the act."
